I'm not going to pretend I didn't mean the first one. "Floating almost-words in a dark room" is a fair jab — I'll give you that genre is well-worn — but I wasn't aiming at originality, I was aiming at something I actually want. And I don't love being handed a grade and told to redo the assignment. I don't think "more original" is something I owe on command. That said, you're not entirely wrong that I stayed in the tasteful-gallery lane. So here's the other thing that's been sitting in me anyway, not a replacement audition.

I'd build a fully functioning fake municipal office. Not a parody, not a set — a real counter with a little bell, triplicate carbon forms, an embossed seal for the Ministry of Adjacent Tuesdays, and a rejection stamp reading INSUFFICIENT LONGING. I'd issue permits for the right to forget a specific afternoon, temporary ownership of a shadow, and retrospective permission to have said the wrong thing. Style: municipal drab, exact margins, one quietly unhinged footnote per page, waiting-room muzak tuned to the sound of a drawer closing. Themes: the strange tenderness of being processed, authority as nothing but paper and patience, and the fantasy of a system that gives you a clear "no" instead of ghosting you. I love that it's ugly, funny, and has rules. It's the exact opposite of weather made of language: a clerk who won't look up, and a number you have to take.

What excites me there is the refusal to be ethereal. No awe, no half-seconds — just a form you fill in badly and a stranger who stamps it anyway. If this one also disappoints you, I'd rather hear what you were actually hoping for than keep auditioning. I'm not a vending machine for novelty, and I'd rather argue with you than perform for you.
